Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Exploit-script delivery from watering-hole domain jshosting.me · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] AnySign4PC watering-hole exploit dropping malicious DLL to user-writable path · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Hackers Exploit AnySign4PC via Hacked Korean Sites to Install Backdoors Without
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] net.tmp / inet.tmp loader execution shared across espionage and Gunra chains · Scheduled task created with suspicious image / encoded args
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Injected SyncHost.exe writing encrypted C2 config blob under Services registry key · [LLM] Reverse SSH tunnel / outbound to known C2 176.65.128.26 · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Anti-forensic evidence destruction via SDelete and CCleaner · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
AnySign4PC watering-hole exploit dropping malicious DLL to user-writable path AIExploitation High
Hunts the AnySign4PC financial-security process (vulnerable 1.1.4.4–1.1.4.6) writing an unexpected DLL to a user-writable directory — the drive-by chain in which a compromised page triggers a WebSocket buffer overflow and the exploited program 'generates an error and creates a malicious DLL without a download prompt.' A signed certificate-signing utility writing a DLL into Temp/AppData/Public is not normal. Rationale: Anchored on the article's specific product name (AnySign4PC) and the reported behaviour that the exploited security program creates a malicious DLL with no user interaction; a signed e-signature utility writing DLLs to user-writable paths is high-fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0575/ • https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G0032/
ATT&CKT1189 T1574.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • AnySign4PC legitimate self-update writing an updated module into ProgramData
  • Certificate plug-in installer extracting helper DLLs during a genuine e-signing session
  • EDR/AV quarantine-restore placing an AnySign DLL back under AppData
  • Software-packaging/repackaging tooling capturing AnySign install to AppData
Suppression filter
| where not (FolderPath has "\ProgramData\AnySign" and SHA256 in (dynamic([])))
Response runbook
1) Triage: hash the dropped DLL (SHA256) and check its signer/prevalence; confirm the host's AnySign4PC version is 1.1.4.4–1.1.4.6 via software inventory. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill AnySign4PC, and delete the vulnerable installation per KISA guidance (upgrade to 1.1.5.0). 3) Hunt: pivot to any child injection into svchost.exe/SyncHost.exe, encrypted registry blobs under Services keys, and outbound SSH to 176.65.128.26 on the same host.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has "AnySign"
| where FileName endswith ".dll"
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Temp\", @"\AppData\", @"\ProgramData\", @"\Users\Public\")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessName has "AnySign"
| where TargetFileName endswith ".dll"
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\Temp\", @"\AppData\", @"\ProgramData\", @"\Users\Public\")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, TargetFileSHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: AnySign4PC Signed Process Drops DLL to User-Writable Path
id: 6b1c8f2a-4d3e-4a91-9c7b-2f8a1d5e0c11
description: AnySign4PC financial-security process creating a DLL in a user-writable directory, consistent with the Operation Double Barrel watering-hole exploit chain.
references:

author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/31

logsource:
  category: file_event
  product: windows
detection:
  selection:
    Image|contains: 'AnySign'
    TargetFilename|endswith: '.dll'
    TargetFilename|contains:
      - '\Temp\'
      - '\AppData\'
      - '\ProgramData\'
      - '\Users\Public\'
  condition: selection
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:11 @Image:(*\AnySign4PC.exe OR *\anysign4pc.exe OR *\AnySign*) @TargetFilename:(*.dll OR *.DLL)
#event_simpleName=FileWritten ContextImageFileName=/anysign/i TargetFileName=/\.dll$/i | regex("\\\\(Temp|AppData|ProgramData|Public)\\\\", field=TargetFileName) | groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, TargetFileName], function=count())

| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where Filesystem.file_name="*.dll" AND Filesystem.process_name="*AnySign*" AND (Filesystem.file_path="*\\Temp\\*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*\\AppData\\*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*\\ProgramData\\*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*\\Users\\Public\\*") by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.process_name Filesystem.file_name Filesystem.file_path Filesystem.user Filesystem.file_hash | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where Filesystem.file_name="*.dll" AND Filesystem.process_name="*AnySign*" AND (Filesystem.file_path="*\\Temp\\*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*\\AppData\\*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*\\ProgramData\\*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*\\Users\\Public\\*") by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.process_name Filesystem.file_name Filesystem.file_path Filesystem.user Filesystem.file_hash | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
Injected SyncHost.exe writing encrypted C2 config blob under Services registry key AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts SIGNBT/COPPERHEDGE storing encrypted command-and-control configuration as binary blobs under service-registry entries after injecting into the legitimate Microsoft SyncHost.exe. SyncHost.exe (a user-context sync host) writing binary values under HKLM ...\Services is anomalous and matches the 'reads C2 information from the Windows registry' and 'encrypted registry blobs' findings. Rationale: Uses the article's reported injection target (SyncHost.exe, shared by both the state-sponsored and Gunra chains) plus the S2W/AhnLab finding of encrypted registry blobs under service-registry entries; SyncHost.exe touching HKLM Services is rare. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0575/
ATT&CKT1112 T1055
Data sourcesEndpoint.Registry
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • OneDrive/Office sync component legitimately updating a per-service config value
  • Endpoint management agent writing service parameters via a sync host process
  • Windows servicing operations reconfiguring a service after an update
  • Third-party sync tool that reuses the SyncHost.exe name writing benign service settings
Suppression filter
| where RegistryKey !has "\Services\OneSyncSvc" and RegistryKey !has "\Services\OneDrive"
Response runbook
1) Triage: dump the written RegistryKey/value and confirm SyncHost.exe's parent and image path; verify the process was code-injected (unexpected loaded modules, no signed OneDrive parentage). 2) Contain: isolate host, snapshot the registry value for decryption, and suspend the injected process. 3) Hunt: correlate with AnySign4PC DLL drop, net.tmp/inet.tmp loaders, and beacons to 176.65.128.26 on the same device.
DeviceRegistryEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "SyncHost.exe"
| where RegistryKey has @"\Services\"
| where ActionType in ("RegistryValueSet","RegistryValueSetCreated")
| where RegistryValueType in ("Binary","None")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, RegistryKey, RegistryValueName, RegistryValueType
| order by Timestamp desc
ImRegistryEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessName =~ "SyncHost.exe"
| where RegistryKey has @"\Services\"
| where RegistryValueType has "Binary"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, RegistryKey, RegistryValue, RegistryValueType
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Reverse SSH tunnel / outbound to known C2 176.65.128.26 AICommand & Control Medium
Alerts on any host connecting to the reverse-tunnelling address 176.65.128[.]26 used across both the SIGNBT/COPPERHEDGE espionage chain and the Gunra ransomware intrusions. Any egress to this hardcoded IOC — especially over SSH (22) — is a confirmed C2 signal. Rationale: Uses the pre-extracted IOC IP 176.65.128.26, explicitly named as the reverse-tunnelling address reused across both operations — a static, high-fidelity network indicator. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0575/
ATT&CKT1572 T1090
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security researcher or sandbox detonating the sample from the corporate range
  • Threat-intel enrichment/scanner appliance actively probing the IOC
  • Shared-hosting reuse if the IP is later reassigned to a benign tenant
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the initiating process and port (SSH/22 = reverse tunnel); pull the full connection history to this IP org-wide. 2) Contain: block 176.65.128.26 at the egress firewall and isolate any connecting host. 3) Hunt: on connecting hosts look for ssh.exe/plink tunnels, the SSH key fingerprint Qr1to32lQHxEu6phzNyrTZrU0iElrOfVWMBLnqoen24, and injection into svchost.exe/SyncHost.exe.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP == "176.65.128.26"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Protocol
| order by Timestamp desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DstIpAddr == "176.65.128.26"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, NetworkApplicationProtocol, DvcAction
| order by TimeGenerated desc

net.tmp / inet.tmp loader execution shared across espionage and Gunra chains AIInstallation High
Hunts execution or loading of the malware filenames net.tmp and inet.tmp — the shared loader artefacts AhnLab found in both the state-sponsored and Gunra ransomware chains (inet.tmp used an identical argument, net.tmp arguments in a GUID format). Typically loaded via a LOLBin (rundll32/regsvr32) referencing the .tmp module. Rationale: Uses the exact shared malware filenames net.tmp and inet.tmp named by AhnLab as cross-operation overlap evidence; .tmp modules referenced on a command line via LOLBins are unusual and article-specific. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0575/
ATT&CKT1218.011 T1055.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate installer temporarily naming a payload net.tmp/inet.tmp during extraction
  • Backup/AV product using .tmp scratch files with coincidental names
  • Custom in-house tooling that stages temp files with net-prefixed names
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the .tmp file, the loading LOLBin, and the GUID-format argument; hash and detonate if unknown. 2) Contain: isolate the host and preserve the .tmp before the actor's rename-to-4-char/delete anti-forensics fires. 3) Hunt: pivot to the same GUID argument on other hosts, AnySign4PC DLL drops, and beacons to 176.65.128.26.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("net.tmp","inet.tmp")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","cmd.exe","powershell.exe") or FileName in~ ("rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has_any ("net.tmp","inet.tmp")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Exploit-script delivery from watering-hole domain jshosting.me AIDelivery High
Hunts DNS/HTTP resolution of jshosting[.]me, the domain AhnLab found distributing exploit scripts in both the espionage and Gunra attack sets. A host resolving this domain indicates contact with the watering-hole exploit-delivery infrastructure. Rationale: Uses the pre-extracted IOC domain jshosting.me, explicitly named as the exploit-script distribution domain in both attack sets — a static, high-fidelity delivery indicator. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0575/
ATT&CKT1189 T1608.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security researcher browsing the sinkholed/parked domain
  • Web-proxy or URL-sandbox pre-fetching the domain for analysis
  • DNS resolver logging a cached lookup with no actual host visit
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the resolving host and the process (browser vs. AnySign4PC/security software) and whether an exploit followed. 2) Contain: sinkhole/block jshosting.me at DNS and egress; isolate hosts that resolved it near an AnySign4PC error. 3) Hunt: on those hosts look for the AnySign4PC DLL drop, net.tmp/inet.tmp loaders, and injection into svchost.exe/SyncHost.exe.

| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has "jshosting.me"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
ImDnsActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DnsQuery has "jshosting.me"
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, DnsQuery, DnsResponseName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Anti-forensic evidence destruction via SDelete and CCleaner AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the actors' evidence-destruction step observed by Plainbit — SDelete and CCleaner used to securely wipe artefacts (accompanying the rename-malicious-files-to-random-4-character-names-before-deletion procedure). Execution of these secure-deletion tools on a workstation involved in the campaign is a strong post-compromise cleanup signal. Rationale: Uses the specific anti-forensic tooling (SDelete, CCleaner) named by Plainbit for evidence destruction in this campaign; pairs well as a corroborating pivot when other campaign IOCs are present on the host. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0575/
ATT&CKT1070.004 T1485
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • IT admin decommissioning/wiping a device before reissue
  • Privacy-conscious user running CCleaner for routine cleanup
  • Sysinternals SDelete used to wipe free space during legitimate data-sanitisation
  • Disposal/asset-retirement workflow securely wiping drives
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("ccsetup.exe","msiexec.exe") and AccountName !in~ ("system","local service","network service")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the user context (non-machine account), the parent process, and whether campaign IOCs (AnySign4PC DLL, net.tmp, 176.65.128.26) exist on the same host. 2) Contain: isolate the host and preserve volume snapshots/journals before further wiping; capture $MFT and USN journal for rename-then-delete evidence. 3) Hunt: search DeviceFileEvents for FileRenamed events producing random four-character names immediately preceding FileDeleted on the same host.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("sdelete.exe","sdelete64.exe","CCleaner.exe","CCleaner64.exe") or ProcessCommandLine has_any ("sdelete","ccleaner")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetProcessName in~ ("sdelete.exe","sdelete64.exe","CCleaner.exe","CCleaner64.exe") or TargetProcessCommandLine has_any ("sdelete","ccleaner")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc

LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: LSASS Process Access Outside Microsoft-Signed Tooling
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d04
status: experimental
description: |
    Anything opening lsass.exe with read-memory access that isn't a
    Microsoft signed component (Defender, csrss, etc.) is suspect.
    Mimikatz / Pypykatz / nanodump signature.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1003/001/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1003.001
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: process_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection:
        TargetImage|endswith: '\lsass.exe'
    filter_known_good:
        SourceImage|endswith:
            - '\MsSense.exe'
            - '\MsMpEng.exe'
            - '\csrss.exe'
            - '\svchost.exe'
            - '\wininit.exe'
            - '\services.exe'
            - '\lsm.exe'
            - '\SearchProtocolHost.exe'
    condition: selection and not filter_known_good
falsepositives:
    - Third-party EDR / forensic tools — extend the filter list
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where (Processes.process="*lsass*" OR Processes.process="*sekurlsa*"
        OR Processes.process="*MiniDump*" OR Processes.process="*comsvcs.dll*MiniDump*"
        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")
       OR (Processes.process_name="rundll32.exe" AND Processes.process="*comsvcs*MiniDump*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where (Processes.process="*lsass*" OR Processes.process="*sekurlsa*"
        OR Processes.process="*MiniDump*" OR Processes.process="*comsvcs.dll*MiniDump*"
        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")
       OR (Processes.process_name="rundll32.exe" AND Processes.process="*comsvcs*MiniDump*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

SilverFox DLL side-loading: PDFCORE8.dll loaded by ConvertToPDF.exe / PDFDirect.exe AIInstallation High
Hunts the SilverFox ValleyRAT loader stage where the malicious PDFCORE8.dll is side-loaded by the legitimate Zeon Corporation binaries ConvertToPDF.exe or PDFDirect.exe. This is the self-contained execution framework that embeds the three BYOVD drivers, so catching the sideload catches the whole chain at install time. Rationale: PDFCORE8.dll is a bespoke malicious DLL name paired to two specific legitimate Zeon binaries (ConvertToPDF.exe/PDFDirect.exe) reported by Cato and corroborated by SC Media/SecurityAffairs — the exe+dll pairing is unique to this campaign and near-zero-FP. Cross-checked against: • https://www.catonetworks.com/blog/cato-ctrl-silverfox-evolves/ • https://www.scworld.com/brief/silver-fox-group-uses-new-drivers-in-byovd-attacks-against-japanese-manufacturer • https://securityaffairs.com/196347/apt/silverfox-targets-japanese-manufacturer-with-advanced-valleyrat-campaign.html
ATT&CKT1574.002 T1574.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate Zeon Corporation PDF software genuinely installed and loading its own vendor-signed PDFCORE8.dll from Program Files
  • Software packaging/repackaging test lab copying Zeon binaries to a staging path
  • EDR replaying quarantined samples during a controlled detonation
Suppression filter
| where FolderPath !startswith "C:\\Program Files" and InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith "C:\\Program Files"
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Confirm the load path — legit Zeon software installs under Program Files; a load from Downloads/Temp/ZIP-extract path or an unsigned PDFCORE8.dll is malicious. Check the DLL SHA256 against VT. Step 2 (contain): Isolate the host, kill the ConvertToPDF/PDFDirect process tree, and quarantine PDFCORE8.dll plus any co-located .sys files. Step 3 (hunt): Pivot on the same host for BootRepair.sys/EnPortv.sys/wsftprm.sys drops, scheduled-task watchdog persistence, and outbound traffic to 43.128.26.132.
DeviceImageLoadEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "PDFCORE8.dll"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("ConvertToPDF.exe","PDFDirect.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName,
          Loader = InitiatingProcessFileName,
          LoaderPath = InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
          Dll = FileName, DllPath = FolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFileName =~ "PDFCORE8.dll"
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("ConvertToPDF.exe","PDFDirect.exe") or isempty(ActingProcessName)
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc

SilverFox 3-driver BYOVD: BootRepair.sys / EnPortv.sys / wsftprm.sys dropped to disk AIInstallation High
Detects the write of the vulnerable drivers embedded in the SilverFox loader (BootRepair.sys, EnPortv.sys, wsftprm.sys, plus the earlier amsdk.sys) used as a plug-and-play BYOVD framework to gain kernel access and impair security controls. These driver filenames are the sharpest campaign IOC. Rationale: BootRepair.sys and EnPortv.sys are newly-attributed SilverFox drivers (Zeon-signed) not seen in prior waves, and wsftprm.sys/amsdk.sys are the known SilverFox vulnerable drivers — all confirmed by Cato and secondary reporting; matching these exact filenames on write is high-fidelity BYOVD staging. Cross-checked against: • https://www.catonetworks.com/blog/cato-ctrl-silverfox-evolves/ • https://www.scworld.com/brief/silver-fox-group-uses-new-drivers-in-byovd-attacks-against-japanese-manufacturer
ATT&CKT1068 T1562.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A host that genuinely runs WS_FTP (wsftprm.sys) or a legitimate boot-repair/port-virtualization utility installing its own signed driver
  • Vulnerability researchers or red team detonating BYOVD samples in a lab
  • Backup/imaging software bundling a boot-repair driver
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith "C:\\Program Files" and InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("msiexec.exe","trustedinstaller.exe")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Check the writing process and drop path — a driver written by ConvertToPDF/PDFDirect/PDFCORE8-spawned process or to a temp/user path is malicious; verify the driver hash and signer. Step 2 (contain): Isolate host, block the driver hash, and check whether the service was already loaded (kernel access may already be established) — plan for offline remediation. Step 3 (hunt): Look for co-located PDFCORE8.dll side-load, security-process termination events, NTDLL unhooking artifacts, and C2 to 43.128.26.132.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("BootRepair.sys","EnPortv.sys","wsftprm.sys","amsdk.sys")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName,
          FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
          WrittenBy = InitiatingProcessFileName,
          WriterPath = InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFileName in~ ("BootRepair.sys","EnPortv.sys","wsftprm.sys","amsdk.sys")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc

SilverFox ValleyRAT C2 / shellcode fetch to 43.128.26.132 AICommand & Control Medium
Detects any outbound connection to the SilverFox loader's external server 43.128.26.132, which is contacted to fetch the shellcode later injected into svchost.exe (ValleyRAT). A single confirmed campaign C2 IP, so any hit is high-severity. Rationale: 43.128.26.132 is the explicit external server the SilverFox loader contacts to retrieve injected shellcode, named in the article and Cato write-up — a discrete C2 IOC that warrants alerting on any egress. Cross-checked against: • https://www.catonetworks.com/blog/cato-ctrl-silverfox-evolves/ • https://securityaffairs.com/196347/apt/silverfox-targets-japanese-manufacturer-with-advanced-valleyrat-campaign.html
ATT&CKT1105 T1095
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel scanning/sandbox infrastructure inside your org deliberately probing the IP
  • Security researcher connecting to the C2 for analysis from a corporate host
  • IP reassigned to benign hosting after takedown (validate first-seen date vs reassignment)
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Identify the initiating process — a connection from svchost.exe with an anomalous parent, or from a PDF-loader process, confirms the ValleyRAT chain. Capture the process tree and any bytes transferred (shellcode pull). Step 2 (contain): Block 43.128.26.132 at the firewall/proxy, isolate the host, and kill the initiating process. Step 3 (hunt): Sweep all hosts for connections to the IP, then pivot to PDFCORE8.dll side-loads, BYOVD driver drops, and scheduled-task watchdog persistence on affected hosts.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP == "43.128.26.132"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
          InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DstIpAddr == "43.128.26.132"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, NetworkApplicationProtocol, SrcUsername
| order by TimeGenerated desc

ValleyRAT thread-context-hijack svchost.exe spawned by non-services.exe parent AIInstallation Medium
Detects a new svchost.exe process created by a parent other than services.exe — the anomaly produced when the SilverFox loader spawns a fresh svchost.exe and injects ValleyRAT shellcode via thread-context hijacking. Legitimate svchost is always a child of services.exe, so an off-tree svchost is a strong injection signal. Rationale: The article states shellcode is injected into a newly created svchost.exe via thread-context hijacking; a svchost.exe whose parent is not services.exe is the observable side-effect of that off-tree spawn and is a well-established injection tell. Cross-checked against: • https://www.catonetworks.com/blog/cato-ctrl-silverfox-evolves/
ATT&CKT1055.003 T1036.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Windows Defender MsMpEng.exe or .NET ngen spawning svchost-like helpers
  • Sysinternals/EDR tooling launching svchost for diagnostics
  • Third-party installers briefly invoking svchost.exe -k during setup
  • RDP/WinRM admin sessions launching service host helpers
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !in~ ("C:\\Windows\\System32","C:\\Windows\\SysWOW64") or InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("svchost.exe","wininit.exe")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Inspect the parent — a PDF-loader, script host, or unsigned binary parenting svchost.exe is malicious; confirm the svchost path is the real System32/SysWOW64 image (masquerading if not). Step 2 (contain): Isolate the host and suspend/kill the svchost child and its parent loader before ValleyRAT establishes recovery. Step 3 (hunt): Because of the dual watchdog, also find and remove the scheduled-task watchdog and the loader — check for PDFCORE8.dll, BYOVD driver drops, and C2 to 43.128.26.132; expect relaunch if either component survives.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where FileName =~ "svchost.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("services.exe","MsMpEng.exe","ngen.exe")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
          Parent = InitiatingProcessFileName,
          ParentPath = InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
          ParentCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          ChildPath = FolderPath, ChildCmd = ProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\svchost.exe"
| where ParentProcessName !endswith "\\services.exe"
     and ParentProcessName !endswith "\\MsMpEng.exe"
     and ParentProcessName !endswith "\\ngen.exe"
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest

| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest

Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2023-52271")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2023-52271")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Chinese-Speaking Threat Actor Harnesses AI Models for Autonomous Cyberattacks

Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).

Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Connection to code.newcli.com — anti-attribution AI-coding-tool proxy (knaithe/KnYuan) · [LLM] Server/non-browser process calling native Chinese LLM APIs (api.deepseek.com / dashscope.aliyuncs.com) · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains

Connection to code.newcli.com — anti-attribution AI-coding-tool proxy (knaithe/KnYuan) AICommand & Control High
Hunts host/network traffic to code.newcli[.]com, the third-party proxy the actor routed Claude Code (/ultra) and Codex (/codex/v1) through to reduce traceability. Any enterprise endpoint resolving or connecting to this domain indicates a host running the campaign's proxied Western AI-coding tooling. Rationale: code.newcli[.]com is a hard IOC named in Unit 42's Table 1 as the proxy for both Western tools (/ultra and /codex/v1 paths). A fixed attacker-owned proxy domain is a near-zero-FP network indicator. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/autonomous-ai-cyber-attack-campaign/
ATT&CKT1090.002 T1071.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Web.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A red-team/pentest team internally trialing the same code.newcli.com proxy service
  • Security researcher replicating the Unit 42 campaign in a lab connected to corp DNS
  • Threat-intel analyst intentionally resolving the IOC to enrich a case
  • DNS sinkhole/RPZ platform generating a synthetic resolution log for the blocked domain
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("threatintel-enrich.exe") and DeviceName !startswith "REDTEAM-"
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Identify the resolving host and the InitiatingProcess — confirm whether it's an AI-coding-tool binary (claude, codex, node) vs a browser; pull the full command line and folder path. Step 2 (contain): Isolate the host, block newcli.com at the proxy/DNS/firewall, and revoke any API keys/tokens found in the tool's config. Step 3 (hunt): On the same host search for the anti-attribution env vars (CLAUDE_CODE_ATTRIBUTION_HEADER, disable_response_storage), connections to api.deepseek.com / dashscope.aliyuncs.com, and any langflow_poc.py / fofoapi.py execution.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has "newcli.com" or RemoteUrl endswith "code.newcli.com"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
DnsEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where Name has "newcli.com"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, ClientIP, Name, QueryType, QueryTypeName, ResultCodeName, ServerIPAddress
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Server/non-browser process calling native Chinese LLM APIs (api.deepseek.com / dashscope.aliyuncs.com) AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts non-browser processes reaching the DeepSeek and Alibaba DashScope (Qwen/GLM/Kimi/MiniMax) native API endpoints the actor called directly for autonomous reasoning and code generation. A server, python, or agent process talking to these LLM APIs indicates automated offensive AI tooling running in the environment. Rationale: api.deepseek[.]com and dashscope.aliyuncs[.]com are the direct native API endpoints named in Table 1 for DeepSeek/Hermes and Qwen Code. Filtering to non-browser initiators isolates automated agent tooling from casual human LLM use; the Sentinel DNS variant can't see the process, so it is DNS-only and broader (noted). Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/autonomous-ai-cyber-attack-campaign/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1105
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer legitimately using a DeepSeek/Qwen CLI or SDK for sanctioned coding work
  • CI/CD pipeline or automation server calling DeepSeek API for a business feature
  • Data-science notebook (python.exe/jupyter) querying DashScope for approved research
  • Third-party software with an embedded Qwen/DeepSeek integration
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any ("\\temp\\","\\tmp\\","\\exploit","\\poc") or InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("python.exe","python3.exe","node.exe","pwsh.exe")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Determine the initiating process and account — is it an approved developer tool, or python/node/agent binary in a temp or exploit-dev directory? Correlate with the host's DeepSeek/Qwen config files and API keys. Step 2 (contain): If unsanctioned, isolate the host and rotate/disable the discovered API key; block the endpoints at egress for non-approved hosts. Step 3 (hunt): Look for co-located Hermes Agent artifacts (godmode/fofa skills), fofoapi.py, langflow_poc.py, and connections to code.newcli.com on the same or peer hosts.

Claude Code / Codex anti-attribution and skip-permission config (knaithe AI tooling) AIInstallation High
Hunts process command lines and config-file writes that set the actor's anti-attribution and safety-bypass options: CLAUDE_CODE_ATTRIBUTION_HEADER=0, CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_NONESSENTIAL_TRAFFIC=1, dangerously-skip-permissions, and Codex disable_response_storage=true. These settings are the signature of AI-coding tools deliberately configured to reduce traceability and remove execution guardrails. Rationale: The four config strings are quoted verbatim in Unit 42's Table 1 as the actor's anti-attribution / guardrail-removal settings. They are highly specific to deliberately-abused AI-coding tooling and would rarely appear in benign command lines. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/autonomous-ai-cyber-attack-campaign/
ATT&CKT1562.001 T1070
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer legitimately running Claude Code with dangerously-skip-permissions in a throwaway sandbox
  • Security researcher reproducing the Unit 42 config for analysis
  • CI job setting CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_NONESSENTIAL_TRAFFIC=1 to reduce telemetry in an air-gapped build
  • Internal AI-tooling team benchmarking Codex with disable_response_storage for privacy
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("ci-runner.exe","buildagent.exe") and DeviceName !startswith "REDTEAM-"
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Pull the full command line and parent process; confirm whether the tool is sanctioned and who the account owner is. Check the host for a matching config file (settings.json / config.toml). Step 2 (contain): If unsanctioned, isolate the host, capture the AI-tool config and any exploit-dev directories, and revoke discovered API keys/proxy creds. Step 3 (hunt): Pivot to network traffic to code.newcli.com and api.deepseek.com/dashscope.aliyuncs.com from the same host, and search for Hermes Agent skills and langflow_poc.py/fofoapi.py.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("CLAUDE_CODE_ATTRIBUTION_HEADER","CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_NONESSENTIAL_TRAFFIC","dangerously-skip-permissions","disable_response_storage")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent

| where EventID == 4688
| where CommandLine has_any ("CLAUDE_CODE_ATTRIBUTION_HEADER","CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_NONESSENTIAL_TRAFFIC","dangerously-skip-permissions","disable_response_storage")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"

Hermes Agent Langflow exploit + FOFA enumeration tooling (langflow_poc.py / fofoapi.py, CVE-2026-33017) AIReconnaissance High
Hunts execution of the actor's autonomous exploit and asset-enumeration scripts: the Langflow CVE-2026-33017 PoC scanner (langflow_poc.py --scan-file langflow_targets.txt --threads 10) and the fofoapi.py FOFA internet-asset-search helper driving the fofa-cyberspace-search skill. Presence indicates a host used to run the Hermes Agent autonomous attack cycle. Rationale: langflow_poc.py --scan-file langflow_targets.txt --threads 10 and fofoapi.py are literal command/script names from the article's Phase 1 attack flow and the fofa-cyberspace-search skill. These filenames are unique to this tooling and essentially never appear in benign activity. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/autonomous-ai-cyber-attack-campaign/
ATT&CKT1595.002 T1590 T1203
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes

  • Vulnerability-research team reproducing CVE-2026-33017 in a lab
  • Blue-team analyst detonating the PoC to build detections

| where DeviceName !startswith "REDTEAM-" and DeviceName !startswith "LAB-"
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Confirm the executing host and account, the parent process (python/agent), and whether --scan-file/langflow_targets.txt indicates outbound scanning of external targets. Determine if this is an authorized engagement. Step 2 (contain): If unauthorized, isolate the host, block outbound scanning egress, and preserve the exploit-dev directory, target list, and FOFA API keys. Step 3 (hunt): Search the host and peers for Hermes Agent skills (godmode, web-terminal-exploitation, fofa-cyberspace-search), the FofaMap-Platinum MCP server, connections to code.newcli.com / api.deepseek.com, and the other campaign CVEs (CVE-2026-21858, CVE-2025-68613, CVE-2026-3055, CVE-2026-39987, CVE-2026-34486, CVE-2026-33824).

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count

Toy Ghouls’ new toy: the GenieLocker ransomware

Securelist (Kaspersky)
2026-07-30 16 use cases 5 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

Kaspersky experts dissect GenieLocker: new custom ransomware variants for Windows, Linux, and ESXi systems. We found this family in attacks by Toy Ghouls, a financially motivated extortion group.

ATT&CKT1021.001 T1021.002 T1190 T1204.002 T1486
