Firefox/Tor renderer (content) process spawning an unexpected child — sandbox escape / RCE AIExploitation Medium
Detects a Firefox content/renderer process (firefox.exe launched with -contentproc) spawning a non-Firefox child process. Renderer processes are sandboxed and normally spawn nothing; a child indicates code execution inside the renderer — the exact CVE-2026-10702 primitive (arbitrary code execution in the browser's renderer process) and the pivot toward the GhostLock kernel stage. Architecture-independent per Nebula, so relevant on desktop Windows/Linux. Rationale: Grounds on the article's core primitive ('arbitrary code execution inside the browser's renderer process') and Firefox's own multiprocess architecture: the -contentproc flag uniquely marks the sandboxed renderer, and a renderer spawning any non-Firefox child is a high-fidelity sandbox-escape/RCE signal that precedes the GhostLock kernel stage. Cross-checked against: • https://www.mozilla.org/en-US/security/advisories/mfsa2026-54/ • https://www.cyberkendra.com/2026/06/one-malicious-link-full-root-access.html
ATT&CKT1203 T1068
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Firefox invoking the OS default handler for a downloaded file or a custom URL-scheme protocol (e.g. opening a PDF/mailto) from a content process
  • WebRTC/native-messaging host or browser extension helper legitimately launched from the content process
  • Third-party AV/DLP injecting into and spawning from firefox.exe
  • Crash-handling helpers not in the exclusion list on niche builds
  • Enterprise browser-management agents shelling out from Firefox context
Suppression filter
| where ChildProcess !in~ ("AcroRd32.exe","msedge.exe","chrome.exe") and ChildPath !has "\\Program Files"
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the child process image, path and command line — LOLBins (cmd, powershell, sh, /tmp payloads) or unsigned binaries from the renderer are near-certain true positives; a signed OS file handler is likely benign. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the Firefox process tree, and capture volatile memory for the renderer PID before reboot. 3) Hunt: check the host for CVE-2026-43499/GhostLock local-privilege-escalation activity (unexpected root/SYSTEM child from the same tree), review proxy logs for the malicious page visited immediately prior, and confirm Firefox/Tor build against the vulnerable-version UCs.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "firefox.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "-contentproc"   // the sandboxed renderer/content child
| where FileName !in~ ("firefox.exe","plugin-container.exe","updater.exe","crashreporter.exe","pingsender.exe","minidump-analyzer.exe")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, RendererCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, ChildProcess = FileName, ChildPath = FolderPath, ChildCmd = ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActingProcessName has "firefox.exe"
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has "-contentproc"
| where not(TargetProcessName has_any ("firefox.exe","plugin-container.exe","updater.exe","crashreporter.exe","pingsender.exe","minidump-analyzer.exe"))
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, RendererCmd = ActingProcessCommandLine, ChildProcess = TargetProcessName, ChildCmd = TargetProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Firefox Renderer Content Process Spawning Unexpected Child
id: 5f2a1c94-7b6e-4a2d-9e3f-1c8d0a4b7e21
description: A Firefox content/renderer process (firefox.exe with -contentproc) spawns a non-Firefox child, indicating code execution inside the sandboxed renderer consistent with CVE-2026-10702 (IonStack stage 1).
references:
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/researchers-show-single-malicious.html
  - https://www.mozilla.org/en-US/security/advisories/mfsa2026-54/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/29
tags:
  - attack.t1203
  - attack.t1068
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection:
    ParentImage|endswith: '\firefox.exe'
    ParentCommandLine|contains: '-contentproc'
  filter_helpers:
    Image|endswith:
      - '\firefox.exe'
      - '\plugin-container.exe'
      - '\updater.exe'
      - '\crashreporter.exe'
      - '\pingsender.exe'
      - '\minidump-analyzer.exe'
  condition: selection and not filter_helpers
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @ParentImage:(*\firefox.exe OR *\Firefox.exe) @ParentCommandLine:*-contentproc* -@Image:(*\firefox.exe OR *\Firefox.exe OR *\plugin-container.exe OR *\updater.exe OR *\crashreporter.exe OR *\pingsender.exe)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ParentBaseFileName=/firefox\.exe$/i
| regex("-contentproc", field=ParentCommandLine)
| NOT (ImageFileName=/(firefox|plugin-container|updater|crashreporter|pingsender|minidump-analyzer)\.exe$/i)

Endpoint exposed to GhostLock kernel futex LPE (CVE-2026-43499, IonStack stage 2) AIExploitation Low
Surfaces Linux hosts exposed to CVE-2026-43499 (GhostLock), the kernel futex flaw Nebula uses as IonStack's second stage to carry renderer RCE to root. The article explicitly warns that patching Firefox blocks the browser entry point but does NOT patch GhostLock, so this exposure must be tracked independently of the browser fix. Rationale: Uses the article's second CVE (CVE-2026-43499 / GhostLock) and its explicit operational caveat that the kernel flaw persists after Firefox is patched; TVM CVE match gives clean, independent LPE-exposure tracking for the privilege-escalation phase. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/researchers-show-single-malicious.html • https://www.techtimes.com/articles/319914/20260708/public-exploit-turns-15-year-linux-kernel-flaw-5-second-root-attack.htm
ATT&CKT1068
Data sourcesVulnerabilities.Vulnerabilities
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Host kernel already patched but TVM snapshot stale, still showing the CVE
  • Backported vendor kernel (RHEL/Ubuntu) where the fix is applied but version string still matches the scanner's vulnerable pattern
  • Containers inheriting the host kernel version double-counted as separate assets
  • Embedded/appliance Linux where the futex path is not reachable in practice
  • Non-Android Linux hosts with no browser present (exposure real but full IonStack chain not applicable)
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the running kernel is genuinely unpatched (uname -r vs vendor fixed build) and not a backport false match. 2) Contain: schedule/expedite kernel patching; for internet-facing or browser-heavy hosts, prioritise since GhostLock is invoked directly from the browser. 3) Hunt: on exposed hosts, review for renderer-escape activity (UC: Firefox renderer spawning child) and any unexpected transition to root/uid 0 from a user-context process, which would indicate GhostLock was actually fired.

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

title: FakeCaptcha / ClickFix - Clipboard-Injected PowerShell from Explorer

status: experimental
description: |

    user to press Win+R and paste a payload. The result is
    powershell/mshta launched directly from explorer.exe with iex /
    base64 / downloadstring in the command line.

date: 2026/05/02

CISA KEV: CVE-2026-20316 — Cisco Secure Firewall Management Center Use of Hard-coded Password Vulnerability

CISA KEV
2026-07-29 1 use case 0 techniques 2 kill-chain phases detected

Cisco Secure Firewall Management Center (FMC) formerly known as Firepower Management Center contains a use of hard-coded password vulnerability that could allow an unauthenticated, remote attacker to log in to an affected device using a low-privileged account to access sensitive data within the impacted systems. C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc

| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`

| sort - count

ATT&CKT1539 T1555.003

| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"

| where FileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")

| where TargetFileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children Exploitation Medium
Supply-chain trojan signal: legitimate signed binary spawning script interpreters or exotic LOLBins.
ATT&CKT1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
// Replace `"setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe"` with the vendor binaries observed in the
// article (matching shape with the Defender query).
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\rundll32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\regsvr32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\bitsadmin.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Trusted Vendor Binary Launching Unusual Children
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d09
status: experimental
description: |
    A signed vendor binary (in the article's named-vendors list)
    spawning script-host or LOLBin children. Strongest signal when
    paired with a recent CVE / supply-chain advisory naming the same
    vendor.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1195/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1195
    - attack.initial-access
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\wmic.exe'
            - '\bitsadmin.exe'
    selection_parent_vendor:
        ParentImage|contains:
            - '\Program Files\'
            - '\Program Files (x86)\'
    condition: selection_child and selection_parent_vendor
falsepositives:
    - Many — installers and updaters legitimately spawn children. Pin
      the parent path to specific vendor binaries observed in the
      article before alerting.
level: medium

Vulnerable @hypequery/clickhouse (<2.0.2) package install for CVE-2026-54658 AIWeaponization High
Surfaces hosts/containers where the vulnerable @hypequery/clickhouse npm package is present, either via file writes into node_modules/@hypequery/clickhouse or Defender TVM vulnerability inventory for CVE-2026-54658. This is the attack-surface pivot: SQL injection in escapeValue() is only exploitable where versions prior to 2.0.2 are deployed. Rationale: Uses the exact vulnerable package path (node_modules/@hypequery/clickhouse) and the CVE id from the GHSA advisory; NVD/cve.threatint confirm vulnerable versions <2.0.2. Package presence is the necessary precondition for any exploitation. Cross-checked against: • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-54658 • https://cve.threatint.com/CVE/CVE-2026-54658 • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-6wcc-39rp-hh9p
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer workstations that legitimately use @hypequery/clickhouse in dev but not exposed to untrusted input
  • CI/CD build agents restoring node_modules from cache before an upgrade PR lands
  • Security researchers cloning the vulnerable repo for testing
  • Container base-image rebuilds that reinstall the same version pending a patch
  • Internal analytics services already scheduled for the 2.0.2 upgrade
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","npm.exe","pnpm.exe","yarn.exe","node")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the installed SoftwareVersion is <2.0.2 and whether the service passes user-controlled input into hypequery query parameters (check exposure vs. internal-only). 2) Contain: prioritise upgrade to 2.0.2+; for internet-facing services, gate the endpoint behind a WAF rule blocking backslash-quote sequences until patched (do NOT rely on app-side input sanitisation — advisory says the library must fix escaping). 3) Hunt: pivot to UC-2/UC-3 to check whether any exploitation attempts (backslash-quote payloads) already hit this host, and inventory all other hosts/images carrying the package.

| where FolderPath has @"node_modules\@hypequery\clickhouse" or FolderPath has "node_modules/@hypequery/clickhouse"
| where FileName =~ "package.json"

CVE-2026-54658 SQL injection: trailing backslash quote-escape payload in web/proxy request parameters AIExploitation Medium
Hunts the specific exploitation primitive from CVE-2026-54658 — a parameter value using a trailing backslash to escape the closing single quote (\') followed by injected SQL — inside HTTP request query strings captured by WAF/proxy or web-tier logs. This is the on-the-wire signature of the escapeValue() bypass, not a generic SQLi template. Rationale: Targets the advisory's exact mechanism — 'a trailing backslash to escape the closing quote' — as the \'(-encoded %5c%27) sequence immediately preceding SQL keywords, which is far more specific than generic OR-1=1 SQLi. Payloads in POST/JSON/gRPC bodies won't appear in URL query strings (noted limitation); pair with UC-3 for backend confirmation. Defender endpoint telemetry has no HTTP request-parameter source, so defender_kql is intentionally blank. Cross-checked against: • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-54658 • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-6wcc-39rp-hh9p
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesWeb.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate URLs containing Windows file paths that end in a backslash before a quoted token
  • Security scanners (Burp/ZAP/Nuclei) running authorized SQLi test suites against the app
  • Regex-heavy application parameters that naturally contain 'or'/'select' substrings adjacent to escaped characters
  • Marketing/analytics query strings with URL-encoded punctuation that coincidentally matches
  • WAF already blocking and re-logging the same payload multiple times per request
Suppression filter
| where RequestURL matches regex @"(?i)(union(%20|\+|\s)+select|;(%20|\+|\s)*(drop|insert|update|delete)|--|/\*)"
Response runbook
1) Triage: decode the RequestURL, confirm the \'-then-SQL structure targets a hypequery-backed endpoint, and check the source IP's request history for enumeration/fuzzing bursts. 2) Contain: block the source IP at the WAF, add a rule rejecting backslash-immediately-before-quote in parameters, and confirm the target service is on @hypequery/clickhouse 2.0.2+. 3) Hunt: correlate the request timestamp against UC-3 ClickHouse query-log/syntax-error events on the backend, and review DB audit logs for successful UNION/stacked queries or data reads following the request.
CommonSecurityLog

| where isnotempty(RequestURL)
| where RequestURL matches regex @"(?i)(%5c|\\)(%27|')(?:%20|\+|\s)*(or|union|select|and|;|--|%3b)"
| project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, DestinationIP, DestinationHostName, RequestMethod, RequestURL, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct
| order by TimeGenerated desc

goshs running --no-delete deletes/renames files on disk (CVE-2026-64863 MOVE bypass) AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts the actual data-loss primitive: a goshs process launched with the --no-delete guard that nonetheless performs file rename/delete operations on disk. Under the CVE, a WebDAV MOVE renames (deletes) the source and, with Overwrite:T, RemoveAll's the destination — so any FileDeleted/FileRenamed initiated by a goshs '--no-delete' instance is the bypass executing. Rationale: Binds the two article-specific strings that together prove exploitation: the process image 'goshs' AND the '--no-delete' flag it was launched with, correlated to an actual FileDeleted/FileRenamed. A no-delete instance deleting files is the CVE by definition — near-zero benign overlap.
ATT&CKT1485 T1070.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Operator legitimately using the goshs UPLOAD or unrestricted mode (no --no-delete flag) — excluded by the cmdline filter
  • goshs writing/overwriting freshly uploaded files in an allowed upload dir (FileWritten, not delete)
  • Antivirus/EDR quarantining a file goshs just wrote, showing as a delete on the same path
  • Log-rotation or temp-file cleanup by a wrapper script that happens to share the goshs working dir
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("--upload-only","-uo") and ActionType == "FileCreated")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the goshs cmdline actually contains --no-delete and identify the deleted/renamed FolderPath+PreviousFolderPath — a rename to an unrelated name or a delete of a served artifact confirms abuse. 2) Contain: stop the goshs service and block its listening WebDAV port at the host firewall; snapshot the served directory for recovery. 3) Hunt: pull the WebDAV access log for MOVE requests around the file event, extract source IPs, and search for the same client issuing PROPFIND enumeration or repeated MOVE calls across other goshs hosts.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "goshs"
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "--no-delete"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileDeleted")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FolderPath, PreviousFolderPath, FileName, PreviousFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessId
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActingProcessName has "goshs"
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has "--no-delete"
| where EventType in ("FileDeleted","FileRenamed","FileModified")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ActorUsername
| order by TimeGenerated desc

WebDAV MOVE succeeds (201/204) against goshs --no-delete server AIExploitation Medium
Hunts the wire-side signature of the bypass: a WebDAV MOVE verb returning 201 Created or 204 No Content. Under a correctly enforced --no-delete policy MOVE should be 403; a successful MOVE is the source-file deletion (rename) primitive the CVE exposes on the goshs WebDAV port. Rationale: Keys on the exact article verb+status: MOVE returning 201/204. Successful WebDAV MOVE is rare in most estates and is the documented deletion primitive; scoping to the goshs host (by DstIpAddr/port) turns it high-fidelity.
ATT&CKT1190 T1485
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate WebDAV clients (macOS Finder, Windows Explorer web folders, Cyberduck) that use MOVE for normal rename operations on an intended-writable share
  • A goshs instance intentionally run WITHOUT --no-delete where MOVE is expected
  • Backup or sync tooling that stages files via MOVE/rename over WebDAV
  • Automated CI artifact reorganisation against a non-protected goshs endpoint
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm DstIpAddr/port is a goshs --no-delete instance (check the host's process cmdline) and inspect the MOVE Url + Destination to see which served file was renamed away. 2) Contain: restrict the WebDAV port to trusted source IPs or take goshs offline until upgraded past v2.1.3. 3) Hunt: from the source IP, enumerate all MOVE/DELETE/PROPFIND to the same host and correlate to host-side FileDeleted events (see the goshs file-deletion UC) to confirm data loss.
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where HttpMethod =~ "MOVE"
| where toint(HttpStatusCode) in (201, 204)
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, DstHostname, DstPortNumber, Url, HttpMethod, HttpStatusCode, HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent
| order by TimeGenerated desc

WebDAV --no-delete probe: 403 DELETE then successful MOVE on same path AIExploitation High
Detects the exploit's discovery-to-abuse pivot described verbatim in the advisory: DELETE is blocked (403) but MOVE on the same resource succeeds. Correlating a 403 DELETE followed within 60s by a 201/204 MOVE on the identical URL from the same client is the bypass signature. Rationale: Directly encodes the advisory's stated asymmetry ('DELETE is correctly blocked (403) but MOVE still destroys files') as a same-URL, same-client 403-DELETE→2xx-MOVE temporal correlation — an operational sequence with essentially no benign explanation.
ATT&CKT1190 T1211
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A WebDAV client that retries a failed delete as a rename by design (rare, but some sync tools fall back)
  • Two unrelated users hitting the same URL where one's DELETE is denied by ACL and another legitimately renames — mitigated by same-SrcIpAddr join
  • Load-balancer health probes issuing method variety (won't produce 403+2xx on same file path)
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full request sequence from SrcIpAddr to DstHostname — a 403 DELETE immediately followed by a 2xx MOVE on the same Url is a deliberate probe; note the Destination header target. 2) Contain: block SrcIpAddr at the WAF/proxy and restrict the goshs WebDAV port; preserve the served directory for recovery. 3) Hunt: sweep all goshs hosts for the same source IP and for host-side FileDeleted/FileRenamed by goshs to quantify data destroyed.
let win = 60s;
let moves = ImWebSession
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where HttpMethod =~ "MOVE" and toint(HttpStatusCode) in (201,204)
    | project MoveTime = TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, DstHostname, Url;
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where HttpMethod =~ "DELETE" and toint(HttpStatusCode) == 403
| project DelTime = TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, DstHostname, Url
| join kind=inner moves on SrcIpAddr, DstHostname, Url
| where MoveTime between (DelTime .. DelTime + win)
| extend DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', MoveTime, DelTime)
| project DelTime, MoveTime, DelaySec, SrcIpAddr, DstHostname, Url
| order by MoveTime desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count from datamodel=Web.Web where Web.http_method IN ("DELETE","MOVE") by _time, Web.src, Web.dest, Web.url, Web.http_method, Web.status span=1s | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` | eval isDenyDelete=if(http_method="DELETE" AND status==403,1,0), isMove=if(http_method="MOVE" AND (status==201 OR status==204),1,0) | stats max(eval(if(isDenyDelete==1,_time,null()))) as delTime max(eval(if(isMove==1,_time,null()))) as moveTime values(status) as statuses by src, dest, url | where isnotnull(delTime) AND isnotnull(moveTime) AND moveTime>=delTime AND (moveTime-delTime)<=60 | eval delaySec=moveTime-delTime | sort - moveTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Web.Web where Web.http_method IN ("DELETE","MOVE") by _time, Web.src, Web.dest, Web.url, Web.http_method, Web.status span=1s | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` | eval isDenyDelete=if(http_method="DELETE" AND status==403,1,0), isMove=if(http_method="MOVE" AND (status==201 OR status==204),1,0) | stats max(eval(if(isDenyDelete==1,_time,null()))) as delTime max(eval(if(isMove==1,_time,null()))) as moveTime values(status) as statuses by src, dest, url | where isnotnull(delTime) AND isnotnull(moveTime) AND moveTime>=delTime AND (moveTime-delTime)<=60 | eval delaySec=moveTime-delTime | sort - moveTime
WebDAV MOVE with Overwrite:T header (destructive RemoveAll on destination) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts the second, more destructive bypass path: a WebDAV MOVE carrying the 'Overwrite: T' header, which makes golang.org/x/net/webdav RemoveAll the existing destination before renaming — clobbering a pre-existing victim file even under --no-delete. Requires WAF/proxy header capture. Rationale: Targets the exact header the advisory names as the overwrite mechanism ('with Overwrite: T it additionally performs an explicit RemoveAll on the destination'). MOVE+Overwrite:T is the destructive-clobber variant and is not a shape normal clients emit against a read-controlled share.
ATT&CKT1190 T1485
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • macOS Finder / Windows mini-redirector legitimately sending Overwrite:T on renames against an intentionally writable WebDAV share
  • Sync clients (Cyberduck, davfs2) that default Overwrite:T on rename
  • Proxy not capturing request headers → query silently returns nothing (coverage gap, not a benign hit)
  • A goshs instance run without --no-delete where overwrite is expected behaviour
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the target DestinationHostName is a goshs --no-delete instance and read the Destination header to see which existing file was RemoveAll'd. 2) Contain: block the SourceIP and restrict the WebDAV port; recover the clobbered file from backup/snapshot. 3) Hunt: correlate to host-side FileDeleted+FileWritten to the same path by the goshs process, and search other goshs hosts for MOVE+Overwrite:T from the same client.
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where RequestMethod =~ "MOVE"
| where Message has "Overwrite: T" or Message has "Overwrite:T" or DeviceCustomString1 has "Overwrite" or RequestContext has "Overwrite"
| project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, DestinationIP, DestinationHostName, RequestURL, RequestMethod, RequestClientApplication, Message, DeviceCustomString1
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Vulnerable goshs exposure: process launched with --webdav and --no-delete (<= v2.1.3) AIWeaponization High
Inventory/exposure hunt for the vulnerable configuration itself: any goshs process started with both --webdav and --no-delete is exploitable by CVE-2026-64863 until upgraded past v2.1.3 (commit ba00ce3). Surfaces the attack surface before it is abused. Rationale: Uses the two flags the advisory names as the vulnerable combination (--webdav + --no-delete) plus the binary name goshs; projecting ProcessVersionInfoProductVersion lets an analyst confirm <= 2.1.3 without hand-editing the query.
ATT&CKT1190 T1592.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A goshs instance already upgraded past v2.1.3 where the flag combo is present but patched — check ProcessVersionInfoProductVersion
  • Internal-only goshs on a segmented network with no untrusted WebDAV clients (still vulnerable, lower priority)
  • Security team running goshs deliberately for a lab/CTF exercise
  • A renamed goshs binary — mitigated by also matching via the --no-delete/--webdav cmdline tokens
Suppression filter
| where ProcessVersionInfoProductVersion !in ("2.1.4","2.2.0") or isempty(ProcessVersionInfoProductVersion)
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the goshs version (ProcessVersionInfoProductVersion / --version) is <= 2.1.3 and determine whether the WebDAV port is reachable from untrusted networks. 2) Contain: upgrade goshs past 2.1.3, or firewall the WebDAV port to trusted hosts as an interim control. 3) Hunt: for every exposed instance, review WebDAV access logs for MOVE/Overwrite:T activity and host-side goshs file deletions to determine if the bypass was already used.

| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "goshs"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "--webdav" and ProcessCommandLine has "--no-delete"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, ProcessVersionInfoProductVersion, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate

| where TargetProcessName has "goshs"
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has "--webdav" and TargetProcessCommandLine has "--no-delete"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc

goshs vulnerable SFTP config: -sftp with empty-credential -b and no keyfile (CVE-2026-62325) AIExploitation High
Hunts for the goshs process being started with the SFTP subsystem enabled and basic-auth (`-b`) containing an empty username or empty password segment while no keyfile (`-fkf`) is supplied. This exact combination causes gliderlabs/ssh to fall back to NoClientAuth=true, granting unauthenticated SFTP file access as described in the advisory. Rationale: Uses the advisory's exact reproduction string `-b 'admin:' -sftp` with no `-fkf`: the regex catches both the empty-password (`admin:`) and empty-username (`:pass`) variants, and excluding `-fkf` isolates the vulnerable NoClientAuth path. Cross-checked GHSA-rjrw-mjq6-hpmm and the prior GHSA-c29w-qq4m-2gcv it incompletely fixes. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-rjrw-mjq6-hpmm • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-c29w-qq4m-2gcv
ATT&CKT1190 T1133
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Authorized red-team/pentest engagement standing up goshs for quick file transfer
  • CTF or lab environment intentionally reproducing CVE-2026-62325
  • Security researcher validating the advisory PoC
  • DevOps engineer using goshs as an internal passwordless file drop behind a firewall
  • goshs started with a legit `-b user:pass` where the password happens to contain a trailing space (rare parsing edge)
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "pentest" and FolderPath !startswith "/opt/labs/"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the goshs cmdline truly has an empty credential segment and no `-fkf`, and identify the listening port and whether the host is internet-facing. 2) Contain: kill the goshs process and block inbound to its SFTP port at the host/edge firewall; if internet-facing, treat any served files as exposed. 3) Hunt: pull inbound connections to that port and file read/write events by the goshs PID to scope what was accessed or planted, and search other hosts for the same vulnerable invocation.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName has "goshs" or ProcessCommandLine has "goshs"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "-sftp" and ProcessCommandLine has "-b"
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)-b\s+([^\s:]+:(\s|$)|:[^\s]+)"
| where ProcessCommandLine !has "-fkf"
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where TargetProcessName has "goshs" or TargetProcessCommandLine has "goshs"
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has "-sftp" and TargetProcessCommandLine has "-b"
| where TargetProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)-b\s+([^\s:]+:(\s|$)|:[^\s]+)"
| where TargetProcessCommandLine !has "-fkf"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

goshs launched with empty-credential -b basic auth (empty user or pass segment) AIInstallation Medium
Broad hunt for any goshs invocation whose `-b` basic-auth argument has an empty username (`:pass`) or empty password (`user:`) segment without a keyfile, regardless of whether `-sftp` is present. Complements the combined-flag alert by catching the misconfiguration itself, including future input variants of the unfixed `&&` root cause. Rationale: Directly encodes the advisory's two exploitable input formats `-b 'admin:'` (empty password) and `-b ':pass'` (empty username) via a single regex, and excludes the `-fkf` keyfile flag whose presence installs a PublicKeyHandler and closes the NoClientAuth path. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-rjrw-mjq6-hpmm • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-c29w-qq4m-2gcv
ATT&CKT1190 T1078
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Admin deliberately running goshs with only a username for an internal HTTP share (SFTP not enabled)
  • Red-team tooling directory containing goshs test invocations
  • Automation/CI that spins up goshs with placeholder credentials for smoke tests
  • Documentation or training material commands captured by EDR shell logging
Suppression filter
| where ProcessCommandLine !has "-sftp" and DeviceName !startswith "lab-"
Response runbook
1) Triage: determine whether `-sftp` is also present (SFTP + empty cred = unauthenticated file access) versus HTTP-only, and check the host's exposure. 2) Contain: stop the process if SFTP is enabled or the host is internet-facing; otherwise flag the owner to add `-fkf` or full credentials. 3) Hunt: sweep the fleet for the same goshs binary and cmdline pattern and review file-transfer telemetry from any long-running instances.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName has "goshs" or ProcessCommandLine has "goshs"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "-b"
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)-b\s+([^\s:]+:(\s|$)|:[^\s]+)"
| where ProcessCommandLine !has "-fkf"
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetProcessName has "goshs" or TargetProcessCommandLine has "goshs"
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has "-b"
| where TargetProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)-b\s+([^\s:]+:(\s|$)|:[^\s]+)"
| where TargetProcessCommandLine !has "-fkf"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

File read/write by goshs SFTP server process (post auth-bypass collection) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects file create/modify/delete/rename operations whose initiating process is a goshs instance running with `-sftp`. After the empty-credential bypass, the goshs process itself performs all SFTP file I/O, so its filesystem activity is the collection-phase signal of an attacker reading or planting files. Rationale: Because goshs serves the SFTP subsystem in-process, attributing file create/modify/delete events to a goshs process running with `-sftp` (the advisory's exploited mode) surfaces exactly the read/write/delete/rename impact the advisory lists, with no reliance on unconfirmed IOCs. Sigma omitted: this is a cross-table/aggregation detection, not single-event shape. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-rjrw-mjq6-hpmm
ATT&CKT1021.004 T1105
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate authorized file transfers to an intentionally-run goshs SFTP share
  • Backup or sync job writing through a sanctioned goshs instance
  • Pentest data staging during an approved engagement
  • Developer testing SFTP upload/download against a local goshs server
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "-fkf"
Response runbook
1) Triage: review the file paths written/read by the goshs PID and whether the served directory contains sensitive data or newly planted executables. 2) Contain: terminate the goshs process, isolate the host if unknown files were written, and preserve the served directory for forensics. 3) Hunt: correlate inbound SFTP connections to the goshs port with external source IPs, and check other hosts for goshs `-sftp` processes writing to unexpected paths.

| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "-sftp"
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed","FileDeleted")
| summarize FileCount = dcount(FolderPath), Files = make_set(FolderPath, 25), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessId, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by LastSeen desc

Anomalous Host header on Poweradmin OIDC/SAML/logout endpoints (CVE-2026-54588) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts CVE-2026-54588 exploitation: requests to Poweradmin's /oidc/callback, SAML ACS/SLO, or /logout endpoints carrying an HTTP Host header value that has never been seen for that site in the 30-day baseline. Poweradmin embeds HTTP_HOST verbatim into the redirect_uri/ACS URL sent to the IdP, so an attacker-controlled Host value is the exploitation primitive. Rationale: Uses the article's exact vulnerable endpoints (/oidc/callback, SAML ACS/SLO, LogoutController) and the root-cause primitive (untrusted HTTP_HOST embedded in callback URLs). Baseline anti-join surfaces the attacker's poisoned Host (e.g. attacker.com) without hardcoding the victim's legit hostname. Cross-checked GHSA-3735-5339-xfwx and SentinelOne/NVD (CWE-20/601, CVSS 9.6). Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/poweradmin/poweradmin/security/advisories/GHSA-3735-5339-xfwx • https://www.sentinelone.com/vulnerability-database/cve-2026-54588/ • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-54588
ATT&CKT1190 T1656
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate new vhost/hostname added to the Poweradmin front-end (rename, new DNS name, migration)
  • Uptime/health-check probes (Pingdom, StatusCake) that send synthetic Host headers
  • Load-balancer or Kubernetes ingress health probes hitting endpoints with pod-IP Host values
  • Vulnerability scanners run by the org's own security team (Nessus/Burp) sending crafted Host headers
  • CDN/WAF origin pulls that rewrite the Host to an internal origin name
Suppression filter
| where CsHost !in~ ("localhost","127.0.0.1") and CsHost !endswith ".internal" and CsHost !endswith ".svc.cluster.local" and not (CsUserAgent has_any ("Pingdom","StatusCake","kube-probe","ELB-HealthChecker"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull all requests to the anomalous CsHost on the auth endpoints; confirm the Host value is not an owned domain and check whether the request produced a 301/302 to an IdP authorize URL (redirect_uri would contain the attacker host). 2) Contain: set interface.base_url in Poweradmin config/settings.php (activates the safe branch immediately) and upgrade to 4.2.4/4.3.3; fix the reverse proxy so it does not pass proxy_set_header Host $http_host. 3) Hunt: check the IdP for AADSTS50011 redirect_uri-mismatch events and any successful admin sign-ins in the hour that followed; audit PowerDNS zones (MX, SPF/DKIM, CAA, delegation) for unauthorized changes.
let LookbackDays = 30d;
let RecentHours = 24h;
let AuthPaths = dynamic(["/oidc/","/saml","/logout"]);
let Baseline = AppServiceHTTPLogs
    | where TimeGenerated between (ago(LookbackDays) .. ago(RecentHours))
    | where CsUriStem has_any (AuthPaths)
    | summarize by CsHost;
AppServiceHTTPLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(RecentHours)
| where CsUriStem has_any (AuthPaths)
| where isnotempty(CsHost)
| join kind=leftanti Baseline on CsHost
| summarize FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), Requests=count(), SampleUri=any(CsUriStem), SrcIPs=make_set(CIp,20), Statuses=make_set(ScStatus,10) by CsHost
| order by FirstSeen desc

| eventstats sum(count) as total by uri_path

Host header fuzzing burst against Poweradmin auth endpoints from single source AIReconnaissance Medium
Detects unauthenticated reconnaissance/injection probing for CVE-2026-54588: a single source IP hitting Poweradmin OIDC/SAML/logout endpoints with 2+ distinct HTTP Host header values inside a 10-minute window. This is the shape of an attacker enumerating which flow reflects HTTP_HOST into the outbound redirect_uri. Rationale: Self-contained fan-out on the article's specific auth endpoints; multiple distinct Host headers from one IP is the unambiguous signature of host-header injection probing described in the advisory (unauthenticated, no credentials required). No allowlist/placeholder needed. Thresholds (2 hosts, 3 requests) are conservative and self-evident from the attack shape. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/poweradmin/poweradmin/security/advisories/GHSA-3735-5339-xfwx • https://www.sentinelone.com/vulnerability-database/cve-2026-54588/
ATT&CKT1595.003 T1190
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Authorized DAST/pentest tooling (Burp Suite Intruder, ffuf, wfuzz) run against the app
  • Blue-team validation of this exact CVE after patching
  • Shared-egress NAT/CGNAT where several legitimate clients appear as one IP and hit different vhosts
  • Multi-tenant reverse proxy fronting several Poweradmin hostnames from one upstream IP
  • Search-engine / SEO crawlers requesting the app under multiple canonical hostnames
Suppression filter
| where not (CsUserAgent has_any ("Burp","ffuf","wfuzz","nuclei","Nessus")) and CIp !in ("10.","192.168.")
Response runbook
1) Triage: list the distinct Host values and URIs for the source IP; benign crawlers use consistent, owned hostnames while injection probing uses external/attacker or IP-literal Hosts and clusters on /oidc and /saml. 2) Contain: block the source IP at the WAF/edge and add a WAF rule rejecting requests whose Host is not an approved value for the Poweradmin vhost. 3) Hunt: correlate this IP against IdP AADSTS50011 events and any auth-code grant/redirect to an external host; confirm interface.base_url is set and the app is on 4.2.4/4.3.3.
AppServiceHTTPLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CsUriStem has_any ("/oidc/","/saml","/logout")
| summarize DistinctHosts=dcount(CsHost), Hosts=make_set(CsHost,20), Paths=make_set(CsUriStem,20), Requests=count() by CIp, bin(TimeGenerated, 10m)
| where DistinctHosts >= 2 and Requests >= 3
| order by DistinctHosts desc

Spike of AADSTS50011 redirect_uri mismatch at IdP (poisoned Poweradmin callback) AIExploitation Medium
Detects the IdP-side footprint of CVE-2026-54588 when the OIDC/SAML IdP is Entra ID: a burst of AADSTS50011 (redirect_uri / reply-URL mismatch) failures on a single application within an hour. Entra rejects the attacker-poisoned redirect_uri (attacker.com/oidc/callback) because it is not a registered reply URL, so a cluster of 50011 on the Poweradmin app is high-fidelity evidence of active redirect_uri poisoning. Rationale: Directly maps the article's exploitation mechanic (poisoned redirect_uri sent to the IdP) to the IdP error it produces. Corroborated by Microsoft Learn / SSOJet: AADSTS50011 'spiking on URIs you never deployed' is the documented signature of an attacker probing crafted redirect_uri values — exactly this CVE. 5/hr threshold separates probing from a single stray config typo. Cross-checked against: • https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/troubleshoot/entra/entra-id/app-integration/error-code-aadsts50011-redirect-uri-mismatch • https://github.com/poweradmin/poweradmin/security/advisories/GHSA-3735-5339-xfwx
ATT&CKT1528 T1190
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Genuine app-registration reply-URL misconfiguration after a Poweradmin upgrade or hostname change
  • A single trailing-slash / http-vs-https typo in the app's configured base_url producing repeated 50011 for legit users
  • Developer/staging instance of Poweradmin pointed at the production app registration
  • Reply-URL propagation lag (~60s) right after an admin edits the app registration
  • Load-balanced deployment where one node has a stale/incorrect base_url
Suppression filter
| where not (SrcIPs has_any ("10.","192.168.") and Users == 1)
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the failing redirect_uri/reply-URL values in the sign-in detail — legit misconfig repeats one owned URL, an attack shows external/attacker hostnames or many distinct URIs. 2) Contain: if attacker hosts are present, treat affected users as at-risk (revoke sessions/refresh tokens for any who authenticated), lock the app to strict reply-URL matching, and force Poweradmin's interface.base_url + patch. 3) Hunt: pivot to successful sign-ins for the same users from new IPs in the following hour (see companion UC), and audit PowerDNS zones for MX/SPF/DKIM/CAA tampering.
AADSignInEventsBeta
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ErrorCode == 50011   // AADSTS50011 redirect_uri / reply-URL mismatch
| summarize AttemptCount=count(), Users=dcount(AccountUpn), UserList=make_set(AccountUpn,20), SrcIPs=make_set(IPAddress,20), FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp) by Application, ApplicationId, bin(Timestamp, 1h)
| where AttemptCount >= 5   // 5+ reply-URL mismatches/hr on one app = probing, not a one-off config typo
| order by AttemptCount desc
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ResultType == "50011"
| summarize AttemptCount=count(), Users=dcount(UserPrincipalName), UserList=make_set(UserPrincipalName,20), SrcIPs=make_set(IPAddress,20), FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated) by AppDisplayName, AppId, bin(TimeGenerated, 1h)
| where AttemptCount >= 5
| order by AttemptCount desc
source:azure.activeDirectory @evt.name:"Sign-in activity" @properties.status.errorCode:50011
CLOUD
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true count values(Authentication.user) as users dc(Authentication.user) as user_count values(Authentication.src) as src from datamodel=Authentication where Authentication.action=failure Authentication.signature_id=50011 by Authentication.app _time span=1h
| `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)`
| where count >= 5
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count values(Authentication.user) as users dc(Authentication.user) as user_count values(Authentication.src) as src from datamodel=Authentication where Authentication.action=failure Authentication.signature_id=50011 by Authentication.app _time span=1h
| `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)`

| sort - count
Victim account takeover: new-IP sign-in within 1h of redirect_uri mismatch (CVE-2026-54588) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Correlates the two halves of a successful CVE-2026-54588 account takeover on Entra: a successful sign-in for a user from an IP absent from their 90-day baseline, occurring within one hour of an AADSTS50011 redirect_uri-mismatch event for that same user. Catches the case where the attacker captured the victim's authorization code via a poisoned redirect_uri and then used it/logged in. Rationale: Implements reviewer suggestion #1 and ties the article's stated outcome ('IdP redirects the victim's authorization code to an attacker' → full account takeover, no credentials) to observable telemetry: a fresh-IP success closely following a 50011 for the same user. Baseline anti-join + 1h temporal window is high-fidelity and article-specific to the redirect-poisoning flow. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/poweradmin/poweradmin/security/advisories/GHSA-3735-5339-xfwx • https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/troubleshoot/entra/entra-id/app-integration/error-code-aadsts50011-redirect-uri-mismatch
ATT&CKT1528 T1550.001
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • User travels / switches to a new mobile-carrier or home IP the same hour a legit 50011 config error fired
  • VPN or corporate-proxy egress-IP rotation introducing a 'new' IP for an existing user
  • New device enrollment where the user re-auths from an unfamiliar network after an app-registration reply-URL fix
  • Roaming user behind CGNAT whose apparent IP changes between the failure and the success
  • Admin testing the app registration (deliberately triggering 50011) then logging in from a lab network
Suppression filter
| where DelayMin <= 60 and NewIP !startswith "10." and NewIP !startswith "192.168."
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the success IP's geo/ASN vs the user's baseline and whether the 50011 FailIP differs; check what the session did next (consent grants, PowerDNS zone edits, mail-flow rules). 2) Contain: revoke the user's sessions and refresh tokens, force password reset + re-MFA, and block the new IP; if the user is a Poweradmin admin, freeze PowerDNS zone changes. 3) Hunt: review PowerDNS for MX hijack, SPF/DKIM additions, CAA removals and subdomain delegation; sweep other users for the same 50011→new-IP pattern and confirm the app is patched (4.2.4/4.3.3) with interface.base_url set.
let Lookback = 7d;
let WindowHours = 1h;
let BaselineDays = 90d;
let UserIpBaseline = AADSignInEventsBeta
    | where Timestamp between (ago(BaselineDays) .. ago(Lookback))
    | where ErrorCode == 0
    | summarize by AccountUpn, IPAddress;
let RedirectFailures = AADSignInEventsBeta
    | where Timestamp > ago(Lookback)
    | where ErrorCode == 50011
    | project FailTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, FailIP = IPAddress, Application;
AADSignInEventsBeta
| where Timestamp > ago(Lookback)
| where ErrorCode == 0
| join kind=leftanti UserIpBaseline on AccountUpn, IPAddress
| join kind=inner RedirectFailures on AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (FailTime .. FailTime + WindowHours)
| project SuccessTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, NewIP = IPAddress, Country, Application, FailTime, FailIP, DelayMin = datetime_diff('minute', Timestamp, FailTime)
| order by SuccessTime desc
let Lookback = 7d;
let WindowHours = 1h;
let BaselineDays = 90d;
let UserIpBaseline = SigninLogs
    | where TimeGenerated between (ago(BaselineDays) .. ago(Lookback))
    | where ResultType == "0"
    | summarize by UserPrincipalName, IPAddress;
let RedirectFailures = SigninLogs
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(Lookback)
    | where ResultType == "50011"
    | project FailTime = TimeGenerated, UserPrincipalName, FailIP = IPAddress, AppDisplayName;
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(Lookback)
| where ResultType == "0"
| join kind=leftanti UserIpBaseline on UserPrincipalName, IPAddress
| join kind=inner RedirectFailures on UserPrincipalName
| where TimeGenerated between (FailTime .. FailTime + WindowHours)
| project SuccessTime = TimeGenerated, UserPrincipalName, NewIP = IPAddress, Location, AppDisplayName, FailTime, FailIP, DelayMin = datetime_diff('minute', TimeGenerated, FailTime)
| order by SuccessTime desc

    | `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)` ]

| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime from datamodel=Authentication where Authentication.action=success by Authentication.user Authentication.src Authentication.app _time span=1h
| `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)`

    | `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)` ]
| table firstTime user src app count fail_count fail_src

OAuth consent / suspicious app grant Actions on Objectives High

Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication CloudAppEvents
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] QR-code PDF phishing attachment resolving to workers.dev / pamconj M365 harvesting page (UAT-11764) · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] OAuth device-code authorization flow sign-in (ARToken/EvilTokens MFA bypass) · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children · Article-specific behavioural hunt — IR Trends Q2 2026: Phishing and weaponized remote management tools drive attack
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Trojanized MeshAgent installed as SYSTEM auto-start service (Sinobi covert C2) · [LLM] Zoho Assist Unattended Agent deployment for headless remote access (Warlock / Storm-2603) · Scheduled task created with suspicious image / encoded args · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Endpoint egress/DNS to UAT-11764 / ARToken IOC infrastructure · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Post-compromise M365 defense-evasion inbox rule creation (UAT-11764 mailbox takeover) · [LLM] rclone data-exfiltration staging prior to Sinobi encryption · [LLM] Mass .SINOBI file-extension writes indicating domain-wide encryption · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement · MFA fatigue / push-bombing · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft)
QR-code PDF phishing attachment resolving to workers.dev / pamconj M365 harvesting page (UAT-11764) AIDelivery High
Hunts inbound emails carrying an auto-generated PDF attachment whose extracted URL resolves to the UAT-11764 credential-harvesting infrastructure (clear90489058903-document.workers.dev or *.pamconj.com) rather than a legitimate M365 host. Article-specific because it keys the generic 'PDF with QR code' pattern to the concrete harvesting domains and the compromised-M365 propagation described by Talos. Rationale: Uses the pre-extracted harvesting IOCs (clear90489058903-document.workers.dev, *.pamconj.com) plus the article's explicit 'PDF attachment containing QR code -> M365 credential page' delivery, anchored on the PDF attachment + extracted-URL join so it only fires on the described lure, not any inbound PDF. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/ir-trends-q2-2026/
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.001
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate vendor invoices/newsletters that happen to host content on *.workers.dev
  • Internal test phishing/awareness campaigns using workers.dev landing pages
  • A genuine SaaS product whose links live on Cloudflare Workers domains
  • PDF newsletters with tracking-redirect URLs that terminate on a workers.dev shortener
Suppression filter
| where SenderMailFromDomain !in~ ("trusted-vendor1.com","trusted-vendor2.com")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the PDF (PdfSHA256), detonate it, and confirm the QR/embedded URL points at the harvesting host; check whether the recipient clicked (UrlClickEvents) and authenticated. 2) Contain: quarantine all messages sharing the NetworkMessageId/subject cluster org-wide, block the harvesting domains at proxy/DNS, and force password + session-token revocation for any recipient who reached the page. 3) Hunt: search for the same sender/attachment hash across mailboxes, look for new inbox rules and anomalous SharePoint uploads on clicked accounts (see UC2), and pivot on internal senders (compromised mailboxes re-sending the lure).
let LookbackDays = 14d;
let HarvestDomains = dynamic(["clear90489058903-document.workers.dev","dashboard-bl.pamconj.com","spx.pamconj.com"]);
EmailEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EmailDirection == "Inbound" and DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
| join kind=inner (
    EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where FileType =~ "pdf" or FileName endswith ".pdf"
    | project NetworkMessageId, PdfName = FileName, PdfSHA256 = SHA256, FileSize
  ) on NetworkMessageId
| join kind=inner (
    EmailUrlInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
  ) on NetworkMessageId
| where UrlDomain in~ (HarvestDomains) or UrlDomain endswith "pamconj.com" or UrlDomain endswith ".workers.dev"
| project Timestamp, SenderFromAddress, SenderMailFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress, Subject, PdfName, PdfSHA256, Url, UrlDomain
| order by Timestamp desc

let LookbackDays = 14d;
let HarvestDomains = dynamic(["clear90489058903-document.workers.dev","dashboard-bl.pamconj.com","spx.pamconj.com"]);

Post-compromise M365 defense-evasion inbox rule creation (UAT-11764 mailbox takeover) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects creation/modification of Exchange Online inbox rules that delete, move-to-junk, mark-as-read, or forward mail immediately after an account is phished — the exact defense-evasion behaviour Talos attributes to UAT-11764 for hiding attacker replies while the campaign propagates via the mailbox's contacts. Rationale: Directly implements the article's 'creating email inbox rules for defense evasion' post-compromise action, scoped to the evasion-signalling rule parameters (delete/move/hide/forward) so it does not fire on benign organizational-signature or vacation rules. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/ir-trends-q2-2026/
ATT&CKT1564.008 T1114.003
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • User legitimately creates a 'move newsletters to folder' rule
  • Helpdesk configuring a shared-mailbox auto-forward for coverage
  • Executive assistant setting delegate forwarding rules
  • Third-party mail add-in (e.g. CRM) programmatically creating filing rules
Suppression filter
| where IPAddress !in ("<corporate-egress-ips-if-known>") | where UserAgent !has "MailboxAssistant"
Response runbook
1) Triage: correlate the rule-creating AccountId/IPAddress against SigninLogs — was the sign-in from a new device/geo or a device-code flow? Read the raw rule to see what it hides/forwards. 2) Contain: delete the malicious rule, revoke sessions/refresh tokens, reset credentials, and enforce phishing-resistant MFA on the account. 3) Hunt: check the account for outbound phishing to internal contacts, SharePoint/OneDrive file staging, and OAuth grants; sweep for the same ClientIP/UserAgent creating rules on other mailboxes.
let LookbackDays = 14d;
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where ActionType in ("New-InboxRule","Set-InboxRule","UpdateInboxRules")
| extend Raw = tostring(RawEventData)
| where Raw has_any ("DeleteMessage","MoveToFolder","Junk Email","Deleted Items","MarkAsRead","ForwardTo","RedirectTo","ForwardAsAttachmentTo")
| project Timestamp, AccountDisplayName, AccountId, ActionType, IPAddress, CountryCode, ISP, UserAgent, Raw
| order by Timestamp desc
let LookbackDays = 14d;
OfficeActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
| where Operation in ("New-InboxRule","Set-InboxRule","UpdateInboxRules")
| extend Params = tostring(Parameters)
| where Params has_any ("DeleteMessage","MoveToFolder","Junk Email","Deleted Items","MarkAsRead","ForwardTo","RedirectTo","ForwardAsAttachmentTo")
| project TimeGenerated, UserId, ClientIP, Operation, Params
| order by TimeGenerated desc

OAuth device-code authorization flow sign-in (ARToken/EvilTokens MFA bypass) AIExploitation Medium
Surfaces successful Entra ID sign-ins completed via the OAuth device authorization flow — the exact MFA-bypass primitive the ARToken PhaaS platform exposes across its 80+ endpoints. Buckets by account to catch device-code fan-out and rare-geo approvals rather than every legitimate device onboarding. Rationale: Keys on ARToken's core capability — 'bypass MFA through the OAuth device authorization flow rather than stealing passwords' — via the deviceCodeFlow marker in AuthenticationProcessingDetails, aggregating per account to expose the multi-flow/rare-geo pattern of a phishing operator. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/ir-trends-q2-2026/
ATT&CKT1621 T1078.004
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate onboarding of IoT/kiosk/PowerShell CLI devices that use device-code auth
  • Conference-room / Teams Rooms device enrollment
  • Developers authenticating Azure CLI on headless build agents
  • Smart-TV or streaming apps signing into corporate accounts
Suppression filter
| where AccountUpn !in~ ("svc-devicecode-kiosk@contoso.com","teamsroom01@contoso.com")
Response runbook
1) Triage: for each flagged AccountUpn compare the device-code IPs/countries against the user's normal sign-in pattern and check what resource/app the token was minted for. 2) Contain: revoke refresh tokens and PRTs, disable the device-code grant via Conditional Access for that user group, and reset credentials if the geo/app is anomalous. 3) Hunt: pivot on the same IPs to other accounts, look for immediate mailbox/SharePoint access, new inbox rules (UC2), and PRT-based non-interactive sign-ins following the device-code event.
let LookbackDays = 14d;
AADSignInEventsBeta
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where ErrorCode == 0
| where tostring(AuthenticationProcessingDetails) has "deviceCodeFlow" or tostring(AuthenticationProcessingDetails) has "Device Code"
| summarize SignIns = count(),
            Apps = make_set(Application, 10),
            IPs = make_set(IPAddress, 15),
            Countries = make_set(Country, 10),
            FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp)
  by AccountUpn
| order by SignIns desc
let LookbackDays = 14d;
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where ResultType == 0
| where tostring(AuthenticationProcessingDetails) has "deviceCodeFlow" or tostring(AuthenticationProcessingDetails) has "Device Code"
| summarize SignIns = count(),
            Apps = make_set(AppDisplayName, 10),
            IPs = make_set(IPAddress, 15),
            Countries = make_set(tostring(LocationDetails.countryOrRegion), 10),
            FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated)
  by UserPrincipalName
| order by SignIns desc

Trojanized MeshAgent installed as SYSTEM auto-start service (Sinobi covert C2) AIInstallation High
Detects a MeshAgent/MeshCentral binary being launched by services.exe under SYSTEM — the covert durable backdoor Sinobi operators used as their primary C2 for ~3 days before encryption. Focuses on the service-install persistence rather than any legitimate interactive MeshCentral use. Rationale: Implements the article's explicit Sinobi TTP: 'trojanized MeshAgent installed as a SYSTEM-level auto-start service.' The services.exe parent + SYSTEM context is the differentiator that separates the persistence install from a legitimate MeshCentral console session. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/ir-trends-q2-2026/ • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/wdsi/threats/malware-encyclopedia-description?Name=Backdoor%3AWin64%2FMeshAgent.MTB
ATT&CKT1543.003 T1219
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • An IT team that legitimately runs MeshCentral for remote support installs the agent as a service
  • MSP-managed endpoints where MeshAgent is a sanctioned RMM
  • Security-testing labs deploying MeshCentral for research
  • Reinstallation/upgrade of an approved MeshCentral fleet
Suppression filter
| where DeviceName !in ("<authorized-meshcentral-hosts>") and SHA256 !in ("<approved-meshagent-sha256>")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the SHA256 against your known-good MeshCentral hash and check whether this host is in an authorized MeshCentral deployment inventory; inspect the service's config/command line for the C2 host. 2) Contain: stop and disable the service, isolate the host, and block the resolved C2 endpoint (WSS/443) at the perimeter. 3) Hunt: pull DeviceNetworkEvents for MeshAgent WSS egress to non-corporate servers, check for RDP/WinRM lateral movement from this host, ntds.dit access, and stage the environment for imminent ransomware (see UC7/UC8).
let LookbackDays = 14d;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where FileName =~ "meshagent.exe" or FileName =~ "meshagent64.exe"
     or ProcessVersionInfoProductName has "MeshCentral"
     or ProcessVersionInfoOriginalFileName has "MeshAgent"
     or ProcessVersionInfoFileDescription has "Mesh Agent"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "services.exe"
| where AccountName in~ ("system","local system") or InitiatingProcessAccountName =~ "system"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
          ProcessCommandLine, ProcessVersionInfoProductName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
let LookbackDays = 14d;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID in (4697, 7045)
| where ServiceFileName has "meshagent" or ServiceName has "mesh" or ServiceFileName has "MeshCentral"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account = SubjectUserName, ServiceName, ServiceFileName, ServiceStartType, ServiceAccount
| order by TimeGenerated desc

#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ParentBaseFileName=/services\.exe$/i ImageFileName=/meshagent(64)?\.exe$/i

Endpoint egress/DNS to UAT-11764 / ARToken IOC infrastructure AICommand & Control Medium
Alerts on any host resolving or connecting to the corroborated campaign IOC domains (dashboard-bl.pamconj.com, spx.pamconj.com, clear90489058903-document.workers.dev). A direct IOC-match tripwire for both the phishing-panel/C2 (pamconj) and QR-harvesting (workers.dev) infrastructure. Rationale: Direct match on the three pre-extracted campaign IOC domains for a low-cost tripwire. Confidence is Medium (not High) because these domains are cited only in the Talos article and were not independently confirmed by a second source during cross-checking — validate before treating a hit as definitive. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/ir-trends-q2-2026/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1102
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security researcher/analyst deliberately browsing the phishing page from a corporate host during triage
  • Sandbox/detonation VM that egresses through corporate DNS
  • Threat-intel enrichment tooling actively resolving IOC domains
  • A future benign re-registration of the pamconj.com domain after takedown
Suppression filter
| where DeviceName !in ("<soc-triage-vm>","<sandbox-detonation-host>")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the initiating process/user; a browser hit suggests a clicked phish, a non-browser process suggests C2/automation. 2) Contain: sinkhole/block the domains at DNS and proxy, and if a user reached the harvesting page revoke their tokens and reset credentials. 3) Hunt: correlate the ClientIP/user to inbound QR-PDF emails (UC1), device-code sign-ins (UC3), and subsequent mailbox rule / SharePoint staging activity.
let LookbackDays = 30d;
let IOCDomains = dynamic(["dashboard-bl.pamconj.com","spx.pamconj.com","clear90489058903-document.workers.dev"]);
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where RemoteUrl in~ (IOCDomains) or RemoteUrl endswith "pamconj.com"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName,
          InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
let LookbackDays = 30d;
DnsEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where Name endswith "pamconj.com" or Name =~ "clear90489058903-document.workers.dev"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, ClientIP, Name, QueryType, ResultCode, ResultCodeName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
